title: A novel CAF-related gene signature for prognostic and immunotherapy response prediction in PDAC based on single-cell RNA-seq and bulk RNA-seq data.
abstract: Increasing evidence shows that cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) contribute to tumor progression, create an immunosuppressive microenvironment, and promote resistance to immunotherapy. However, the CAF-related gene signature in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains largely unexplored. In our study, we constructed a nine-gene CAF-related signature and found that it strongly correlated with the prognosis of PDAC patients in different cohorts. Subsequently, we found that the CAF-related gene signature was associated with the genomic alteration landscape, immune infiltration landscape and responsiveness to immunotherapy. GJB2 had the highest coefficient in our CAF-related gene signature, thus we explored the role of GJB2 in the interactions between CAFs and PDAC cells. The results showed that conditioned medium (CM) derived from the GJB2 knockdown group could suppress the malignant phenotype of PANC1 and MIAPaCa2 cells. In summary, this CAF-related gene signature is useful for prognosis prediction and precision therapy of PDAC patients.

title: Rosmarinic acid combined with cisplatin induces proliferation inhibition of hepatocellular carcinoma.
abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is characterized by high proliferation and metastasis potential and is prone to chemotherapy resistance, which seriously restricts the clinical efficacy of cisplatin (DDP)-based treatment. Rosmarinic acid (RA) is a natural bioactive compound that has shown potential anti-tumor and chemosensitizing effects in preclinical studies. The purpose of this study was to systematically explore the synergistic anti-hepatocellular carcinoma mechanism of RA combined with DDP through network pharmacology, molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulation, and in vitro experimental verification. Network pharmacology analysis identified HCC-related core targets, which were enriched in cell cycle, apoptosis, and tumor metastasis pathways. Molecular simulation results confirmed that both RA and DDP can stably bind to core oncogenic proteins and exhibit good structural stability. In vitro experiments demonstrated that the combination of RA/DDP had a significant time-and dose-dependent inhibitory effect on the proliferation and colony formation of HCC cells. This combination significantly induced cell cycle arrest and apoptosis in Huh-7 cells and inhibited their migration and invasion, outperforming the single-drug groups. This study provides an integrated and preliminary mechanistic exploration of the potential synergistic effects of RA and DDP against HCC, integrating network pharmacology, molecular simulations, and in vitro functional assays. These in vitro findings suggest that RA may enhance DDP sensitivity in HCC cell models. Further in vivo and clinical studies are needed to determine whether RA can serve as a DDP-sensitizing agent and whether these effects translate into clinical benefit in HCC.

title: 3D tissue model to patient atlas: dynamic network topology reveals PDAC chemoresistance bottlenecks.
abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) develops chemoresistance through dynamic cell-state transitions, yet the regulatory network architecture governing drug-tolerant states remains poorly characterised, because static expression snapshots cannot capture how interaction topology evolves along treatment-induced trajectories. We established a 3D PANC-1 tissue model on decellularised porcine intestinal matrix, which reaches patient-like proliferation indices and tissue-niche-specific drug responses, and performed single-cell RNA sequencing across four conditions: control, gemcitabine (GEM), TGF-β1, and their combination. Coupling pseudotime trajectory inference to dynamic protein-protein interaction network analysis, we tracked betweenness centrality continuously across cell-state transitions rather than comparing discrete states. GEM survivors engaged a proliferative programme (E2F1, CDK1, AURKA, TPX2, TOP2A, BIRC5), whereas TGF-β1 induced an independent EMT attractor (SPOCK1, MBOAT2, COL5A1, THBS1, FN1). Where the two converged, an emergent bottleneck appeared: CDK1 betweenness centrality spiked selectively, restrained by CDKN1A (p21) and WEE1, defining an S-phase-persistence state enriched for GEM survivors. Cross-examination in a PDAC atlas of 726,107 cells from 231 patients showed 8.7-fold metastatic enrichment of triple-positive cells. This framework, linking controlled 3D tissue experimentation, single-cell systems analysis and clinical-scale patient data, is applicable to drug resistance across cancer types.

title: Cancer cell-specific FOXP3 licenses MMP19-dependent matrix remodeling and metastatic dissemination in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma.
abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is characterized by a dense desmoplastic stroma and early metastatic dissemination, both of which contribute to its poor prognosis. While forkhead box protein 3 (FOXP3) is best known as a lineage-defining transcription factor in regulatory T cells (Tregs), its aberrant expression in cancer cell-specific FOXP3 (c-FOXP3) may also support tumor-cell-intrinsic progression. Our findings suggest that high c-FOXP3 expression is closely linked to aggressive disease behavior and metastatic progression in PDAC. c-FOXP3 enhanced migration, invasion within three-dimensional collagen-rich matrices, and dissemination in orthotopic models. Integrated transcriptomic analysis, chromatin immunoprecipitation, and wild-type versus binding-site-mutant promoter assays identified matrix metalloproteinase 19 (MMP19) as a direct transcriptional target of c-FOXP3. MMP19 silencing significantly attenuated c-FOXP3-driven migration, matrix invasion, and metastasis. Single-cell sequencing further showed that MMP19 is abundant in cancer-associated fibroblasts but also defines a distinct epithelial pool that is reduced after epithelial Foxp3 deletion. Pharmacological profiling did not identify a validated MMP19-selective inhibitor, whereas the FOXP3-targeting antisense oligonucleotide AZD8701 reduced FOXP3 together with MMP19 mRNA and was accompanied by lower PDAC-cell migration and invasion in vitro. Together, these findings extend the known functions of FOXP3 beyond its classical role in immune tolerance and define a tumor-cell-intrinsic c-FOXP3-MMP19 program that supports matrix-invasive behavior in PDAC and provide preliminary evidence that c-FOXP3 is pharmacologically accessible.

title: Metabolic dysfunctions in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma: Pathogenic mechanisms and therapeutic implications.
abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains a highly aggressive malignancy characterized by a dismal prognosis and profound resistance to conventional therapies. Emerging evidence highlights systemic metabolic dysfunctions including obesity, dyslipidemia, type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), and non-alcoholic fatty pancreatic disease (NAFPD) as critical drivers of PDAC initiation, progression and chemoresistance. This review integrates current knowledge on the intricate interplay between metabolic alterations and PDAC biology, focusing on the therapeutic and chemopreventive potential of repurposed metabolic modulators (specifically statins and antidiabetic agents) and novel metabolic pathway inhibitors currently under clinical evaluation. Statins exert prominent antitumor effects in preclinical models by disrupting the mevalonate pathway, impairing Ras prenylation, and reprogramming cholesterol metabolism; however, epidemiological data regarding risk reduction remain inconsistent. Parallel to lipid pathways, glucose homeostasis dictates tumor behavior. T2DM acts as both a potent risk factor and an early paraneoplastic indicator through new-onset diabetes. Among antidiabetic drugs, metformin attenuates PDAC progression via insulin-lowering and AMPK-mediated pathways, though its survival benefits are often obscured in clinical trials by methodological challenges. Conversely, hyperinsulinemia driven by exogenous insulin or secretagogues exacerbates PDAC risk, while incretin-based therapies yield conflicting outcomes. Notably, novel strategies targeting metabolic vulnerabilities, such as SGLT2 inhibition combined with metformin, show promise in targeting chemoresistant, nutrient-deprived tumor zones. Ultimately, integrating metabolic profiling, prescription history, and molecular biomarkers into clinical practice is essential to advance risk stratification and precision oncology. Overcoming tumor metabolic plasticity in contemporary clinical trials will require a shift from single-node therapies towards rational, biomarker-guided combination strategies.
journal: Pancreatology : official journal of the International Association of Pancreatology (IAP) ... [et al.]

title: Oncogenic RAS as an adaptive signaling ecosystem: context-dependent vulnerabilities and resistance-informed therapeutic design.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Direct RAS targeting has progressed from pharmacologic proof of concept to routine treatment for selected KRAS G12C-mutant cancers. KRAS G12C inhibitors and KRAS G12C-EGFR combinations established allele- and lineage-specific treatment paradigms. More recently, the multiselective RAS(ON) inhibitor daraxonrasib became the first FDA-approved direct RAS-targeted therapy for metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinoma, while the KRAS G12D-directed degrader setidegrasib remains investigational. Target engagement alone, however, does not ensure durable disease control, and the same drug class can perform differently across tumor lineages.
MAIN BODY: This Review develops an adaptive RAS signaling ecosystem model in which allele and isoform biology, membrane organization, feedback architecture, mutant-wild-type RAS crosstalk, co-mutation patterns, chromatin state, epithelial-mesenchymal plasticity, metabolism, spatial heterogeneity, the tumor microenvironment and treatment delivery jointly determine pathway dependence and therapeutic escape. Comparisons among pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, colorectal cancer, lung adenocarcinoma and NRAS-mutant melanoma show how related oncogenic RAS nodes acquire different vulnerabilities in distinct tissue contexts. We integrate direct RAS inhibition with mechanism-guided vertical and horizontal strategies directed at feedback rebound, bypass signaling, cell-state persistence, stromal protection, metabolic adaptation and immune exclusion. We then translate this model into a biomarker-integrated development framework that links serial circulating tumor DNA, modality-matched pharmacodynamic assays, paired tissue sampling, spatial profiling and toxicity-aware scheduling to prespecified, falsifiable treatment hypotheses.
CONCLUSION: RAS dependence is conditional rather than absolute. Durable control will require strategies that match the RAS allele and tumor lineage to the dominant adaptive circuitry, verify that target and pathway suppression persist over time, and maintain sufficient dose intensity to exert biologically effective pressure without disabling antitumor immunity or normal-tissue function.

title: Biomimetic Nanoplatform for Fibrosis Remodeling and Anti-PD-1 Potentiation via Cu+/Ca2+ Ion Dysregulation and TGF-β Inhibition in PDAC.
abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains refractory to immunotherapy, largely due to the dense fibrotic stroma that promotes immune evasion and restricts drug penetration. Here, we report a multifunctional biomimetic nanoplatform (RPm@CC-LY) that simultaneously remodels the fibrotic tumor microenvironment and potentiates antitumor immunity. RPm@CC-LY achieves efficient tumor accumulation and effectively attenuates fibrosis through sustained release of Transforming growth factor-β (TGF-β) inhibitor LY2157299 (LY). Concurrently, intracellular acid-triggered degradation induces Cu+-mediated Fenton-like reactions and Ca2+ overload, leading to oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and tumor cell apoptosis. In parallel, RPm@CC-LY reprograms tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) toward an M1 phenotype and enhances dendritic cell maturation, thereby promoting robust CD8+ T cell infiltration. Notably, when combined with anti-PD-1 (αPD1) therapy, RPm@CC-LY induces a systemic immune response in mice. This work establishes a synergistic nanotherapeutic strategy that integrates fibrosis remodeling with ion interference therapy to overcome the immunotherapeutic barriers posed by fibrosis in PDAC.

title: Mechanisms and functions of the TRIM protein family in digestive system cancers.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Tripartite motif-containing (TRIM) proteins are important RING-type E3 ubiquitin ligases that regulate protein fate and signal transduction through ubiquitin/ubiquitin-like modifications and non-ubiquitination mechanisms. In digestive system cancers, TRIM proteins exert highly context-dependent bidirectional effects. Here, we conceptualize TRIM proteins as signal integration nodes linking ubiquitin-mediated regulation, core signaling pathways, and adaptation to the tumor microenvironment.
METHODS: This structured narrative review synthesizes English-language studies indexed in PubMed between January 2010 and October 2025. It focuses on the structural basis, multilevel regulation, molecular networks, phenotypic functions, prognostic relevance, and therapeutic implications of TRIM proteins in esophageal squamous cell carcinoma, gastric cancer, colorectal cancer, hepatocellular carcinoma, and pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma.
CONCLUSIONS: The modular architecture of TRIM proteins enables diverse substrate recognition and regulatory outputs. Cross-cancer analysis identifies pathway-convergent, phenotype-convergent, and pathway-phenotype bridging TRIM members that translate dysregulation of core pathways, including Wnt/β-catenin, PI3K/AKT, and p53, into proliferative, cell death-related, metastatic, metabolic, and immune phenotypes. Their functional direction is jointly shaped by tumor type, molecular subtype, substrate status, microenvironmental cues, and treatment context. Selected TRIM members show potential as prognostic biomarkers, risk-stratification indicators, and predictors of therapeutic response, whereas most TRIM-targeted strategies remain preclinical. Future studies should clarify ubiquitin-chain-specific regulatory logic, subtype-specific functions, and multilayered networks, while rigorously evaluating the specificity, safety, and clinical applicability of TRIM-directed combination therapies.

title: Mitoxyperilysis-based molecular subtyping identifies SPP1+ macrophages and IL1B as critical mediators of tumor progression and immunotherapy resistance in intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (ICC) is an aggressive malignancy characterized by poor clinical outcomes. Although mitoxyperilysis has recently emerged as a novel form of regulated cell death, the clinical relevance of mitoxyperilysis-related molecular subtypes in ICC remains largely unexplored. This study aimed to elucidate the clinical significance, immune microenvironment features, and potential therapeutic targets of mitoxyperilysis-related molecular subtypes in ICC.
METHODS: Based on the expression profiles of 45 mitoxyperilysis-related genes, ICC patients were classified into two subtypes using consensus clustering, and the robustness of the classification was validated in the independent GSE89749 cohort. Survival analysis, immune microenvironment characterization, single-cell transcriptomic profiling, in vitro/in vivo experiments, and nomogram construction were subsequently performed to investigate the underlying biological mechanisms and therapeutic implications.
RESULTS: Two robust mitoxyperilysis-related molecular subtypes were identified. Patients in the high-mitoxyperilysis subtype exhibited significantly poorer overall survival (OS), and subtype classification remained an independent predictor of adverse prognosis. The high-mitoxyperilysis subtype was closely associated with lymph node metastasis, elevated CA19-9 levels, and KRAS mutation. Furthermore, this subtype demonstrated pronounced inflammatory activation, an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME), increased infiltration of neutrophils and M2 macrophages, and elevated expression of immune checkpoint molecules. Single-cell transcriptomic analysis revealed a marked enrichment of SPP1+ macrophages in the high-mitoxyperilysis subtype, with IL1B and CXCL3 identified as key regulatory molecules. IL1B promoted ICC cell invasion and metastasis. Notably, treatment with diacerein, an IL1B inhibitor, synergized with anti-PD-1 immunotherapy to suppress tumor progression and overcome immunotherapy resistance.
CONCLUSIONS: Mitoxyperilysis-related molecular classification provides a clinically relevant framework for prognostic stratification and prediction of immunotherapeutic responsiveness in ICC. SPP1+ macrophages and IL1B represent potential therapeutic targets, providing a promising strategy for precise diagnosis and treatment of ICC.

title: FATP5 loss in hepatocellular carcinoma cells orchestrates tumor-promoting microenvironment by inducing passive long-chain fatty acid accumulation within tumor-associated endothelial cells.
abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is characterized by severe immunosuppression and metabolic reprogramming, yet the spatial dynamics of lipid flux between malignant and stromal cells remain poorly understood. Here, we identify a profound, type-specific metabolic rewiring in HCC driven by the widespread downregulation of fatty acid transport protein 5 (FATP5). FATP5 deficiency in malignant cells selectively attenuates the uptake of long-chain fatty acids (LCFAs), creating an extracellular lipid surplus that is passively sequestered by neighboring FATP3-expressing tumor-associated endothelial cells (TECs). Within TECs, accumulated LCFAs function as endogenous ligands that activate the nuclear receptor PPARγ, culminating in the robust transcriptional upregulation and paracrine secretion of the chemokine CXCL12. Endothelial-derived CXCL12 subsequently engages CXCR4 on infiltrating CD8+ T cells, inducing PD-1 expression and driving terminal T-cell exhaustion, thereby establishing an immunosuppressive niche that accelerates tumor progression. Importantly, our data suggest that HCC subtypes marked by FATP5 depletion and CXCL12+ TEC enrichment may possess potential therapeutic susceptibility to PPARγ antagonism or anti-PD-1 immune checkpoint blockade. Besides affecting the secretory function of TECs, accumulated LCFAs can impair endothelial barrier function, thereby creating a microenvironment with hematogenous metastasis risk. Collectively, our findings delineate a novel tumor-promoting microenvironment cascade orchestrated by LCFA spatial redistribution, providing a promising mechanistic foundation to support the future development of targeted precision interventions for FATP5-low HCC.

title: Chronic stress activates a hypothalamic vagal circuit to promote hepatocellular carcinoma progression in male mice.
abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma and depression frequently co-occur, yet the mechanisms linking them remain unclear. Here, we show that chronic stress, systemic inflammation, or neuropathic pain are associated with hepatocellular carcinoma progression in male mice. Chronic stress hyperactivates a glutamatergic paraventricular hypothalamic nucleus → cholinergic dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus → liver circuit, increasing intratumoral acetylcholine. Single-cell transcriptomics identifies acetylcholine-responsive Chrna9+ epithelial cells that interact with macrophages through COL1A1/2-CD44-STAT3 signaling to promote CXCL1 production. Acetylcholine also promotes tumor cell proliferation through CHRNA9. Circulating CXCL1 crosses the blood-brain barrier and activates hypothalamic glutamatergic neurons, exacerbating depression-like behaviors and establishing a liver-brain feedback loop. Silencing the hypothalamic vagal circuit, tumor-specific Chrna9 knockdown, or systemic CXCL1 neutralization restrains tumor progression and alleviates depression-like behaviors. These findings identify a neural and immune mechanism linking chronic stress to hepatocellular carcinoma progression in male mice.

title: Discovery of Novel Oral Covalent Inhibitors Targeting Active GTP-Bound KRASG12C with Potent Antitumor Activity.
abstract: Current KRASG12C inhibitors mainly target the inactive GDP-bound state, but clinical efficacy is limited, and resistance mechanisms have been identified. We disclose novel covalent inhibitors that selectively target the active GTP-bound KRASG12C. Starting from a high-throughput screen, we identified a keto-indolizine scaffold featuring an aniline-derived acrylamide warhead that covalently binds Cys12 in the switch-II pocket of active KRASG12C. X-ray crystallography revealed key interactions of acrylamide with GMPPCP's γ-phosphate, stabilizing the GTP state. We present medicinal chemistry efforts leading to the discovery of compound 17, which shows favorable oral bioavailability in preclinical species, exhibiting prolonged disruption of the KRAS-cRAF interaction and downstream ERK phosphorylation in vivo. In a KRASG12C-driven pancreatic cancer xenograft model (MIA PaCa-2), orally administered compound 17 achieved complete tumor regression for up to 45 days with good tolerability. This study establishes a novel class of KRASG12C inhibitors targeting the active GTP-bound state, which may have the potential to overcome some resistance mechanisms.

title: Rapid Single-Cell N-glycosylation Profiling of Circulating Human Immune Cells by Mass Spectrometry Imaging.
abstract: The metabolic fitness of immune cells, reflected in part through glycosylation of surface proteins, is a key determinant of their activation, persistence, and effector responses. A recently developed high-throughput antibody capture cell array platform was further optimized to profile N-glycosylation across bulk cell and single-cell populations of peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs). Using antibodies against lymphocyte, monocyte, and dendritic cell markers (CD4+, CD8+, CD11c+, CD14,+ CD16+, CD3+, CD19+, CD56+, CD68+), N-glycosylation patterns of these immune cell subtypes were mapped across human PBMC cultures from healthy donors and those with pancreatic cancer. In this platform, PDMS stamps coated with targeted antibodies create patterned capture coordinates. Captured single cells are confirmed by brightfield imaging and selected via SoloCell software. Following PNGase F digestion and matrix application for MALDI-MSI analysis, N-glycans are acquired from a single laser burst per cell at a rate of 7.5 cells per second (18,000 cells in approximately 40 min). Sialic acid isomer stabilization by chemical amidation provided resolution of α2,6- versus α2,3-linked sialic acids and enabled detection of larger mono-, di-, tri- and tetra-sialylated glycans at the single-cell level. Bulk- and single-cell analyses showed concordant glycomic organization across immune cell subtypes. Bulk-level N-glycan profiles clearly distinguished lymphoid from myeloid lineages, and at single-cell resolution, healthy donor PBMCs similarly segregated into distinct subtype-specific glycomic clusters. In contrast, immune cell subtypes in pancreatic cancer PBMC converged into a common glycomic landscape, with marker-defined populations becoming highly intermixed. This convergence was accompanied by linkage-specific sialylation shifts, including a predominance of α2,6 sialylation and pronounced enrichment in CD3+ and CD8+ T cells. Together, these findings demonstrate that single-cell N-glycomic profiling extends bulk analysis to resolve subtype-specific differences in disease-associated immune N-glycome remodeling.
journal: Journal of the American Society for Mass Spectrometry

title: Tuning Excited-State TICT Dynamics in Hemicyanine Type I Photosensitizers for Hypoxia-Tolerant Photodynamic Therapy of Cholangiocarcinoma.
abstract: Although photodynamic therapy (PDT) has emerged as a promising treatment for unresectable cholangiocarcinoma, the hypoxic tumor microenvironment severely limits oxygen-dependent Type II photochemical processes, resulting in insufficient reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation and compromised therapeutic outcomes. Therefore, developing Type I photosensitizers (PSs) with optimized excited-state dynamics and efficient hypoxia-tolerant ROS generation is critical for improving PDT efficacy under hypoxic conditions. Herein, we developed three hemicyanine-based Type I PSs (HCy1-3) and systematically investigated the relationship between molecular structure, TICT-mediated excited-state relaxation, and ROS generation behavior. By modulating the electron-donating capability of donor moieties, the TICT characteristics of the hemicyanine scaffold were precisely tuned, thereby regulating the competition between nonradiative decay and ROS-generating pathways. Among them, HCy3 exhibited enhanced excited-state utilization and the highest Type I ROS generation efficiency under both normoxic and hypoxic conditions. Furthermore, HCy3 efficiently accumulated in mitochondria and induced mitochondrial dysfunction, leading to superior photodynamic cytotoxicity against cholangiocarcinoma cells under hypoxia compared with the clinically used PS HiPorfin. The therapeutic potential of HCy3 was further validated in cholangiocarcinoma organoids. This study establishes a structure-photophysics-photochemistry correlation between TICT regulation and Type I ROS generation, providing a mechanistic strategy for designing high-performance hypoxia-tolerant PSs for PDT.
journal: The journal of physical chemistry. B

title: TGF-β-Targeting Platinum(IV) Prodrugs Remodel Tumor Microenvironment of Pancreatic Cancer via Antifibrotic and Immunomodulatory Effects.
abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) features dense desmoplastic stroma that impedes drug penetration and immune infiltration, and promotes therapeutic resistance. As a central driver of stromal fibrosis and immunosuppression, TGF-β represents an attractive target for overcoming these barriers. Herein, we report novel Pt(IV) prodrugs conjugated with TGF-β inhibitors (hydronidone/4-hydroxyphenylacetic acid), which simultaneously achieve chemotherapy and tumor microenvironment remodeling. Biological screening identified HP-12C and AP as lead compounds with tumor-selective cytotoxicity and substantial activity in patient-derived organoids. In vitro, these prodrugs suppressed tumor-cell-derived TGF-β-associated profibrotic signaling, attenuated cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) activation, improved platinum penetration across a fibrotic barrier model; and partially relieved tumor-mediated immunosuppression in PBMC co-culture assays. In vivo, HP-12C showed superior tumor accumulation and antitumor efficacy, reduced fibrosis, favorable tolerability relative to conventional platinum drugs, and increased CD8+ T-cell infiltration. Collectively, these findings identify TGF-β-modulated Pt(IV) prodrugs as a promising chemotherapy strategy to overcome fibrosis and immunosuppressive barriers in PDAC.

title: In Cellulo Observation of De Novo-Synthesized Nucleotide by Spectral Tracing of Glutamine-Derived Nitrogen Metabolism (QN-STIM) in Cancer Cells.
abstract: De novo nucleotide biosynthesis is directly linked to glutamine-derived nitrogen metabolism in mammalian cells. It is a fundamental process tightly tied to cellular growth, proliferation, and metabolic reprogramming, particularly in cancer cells. Direct detection and imaging of glutamine-derived nitrogen metabolism at single-cell resolution remains a challenge. The conventional liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry-based approach for detecting de novo-synthesized nucleotide studies is mostly performed on metabolites extracted from a group of cells, which makes it inherently destructive. Herein, we introduce a vibrational spectroscopy-based single-cell metabolic detection and imaging framework, "glutamine (Q)-derived nitrogen spectral tracing and imaging (QN-STIM)". Using this strategy, we detected and mapped nitrogen flow from glutamine to de novo-synthesized nascent nucleotides at the single-cell level. First, a proof-of-concept analysis was conducted in human embryonic kidney HEK293T cells and demonstrated the feasibility of this approach in cancer cells, namely human lung carcinoma A549, human glioblastoma U87 MG, and mouse hepatoma Hepa1-6. QN-STIM technique holds immense potential to be an adjunct tool to advance our understanding of nucleotide dynamics during differentiation, stress adaptation, and immune activation, and to evaluate responses to metabolic drugs in cellulo.

title: Biomimetic Dual-Driven Janus Nanorobots for Enhanced Penetration and Combined Gas/Photothermal/Photodynamic/Catalytic Therapy of Pancreatic Cancer.
abstract: Pancreatic cancer (PC) remains an extremely lethal malignancy due to its dense desmoplastic stroma and aberrant tumor microenvironment (TME), which severely impedes the efficacy of conventional therapies. Herein, a biomimetic dual-driven Janus nanorobot (rCeGLI@PM) is strategically constructed via the asymmetric decoration of l-arginine (l-Arg)-functionalized and indocyanine green (ICG)-loaded poly(amidoamine) dendrimers onto CeOx nanozymes, followed by homologous Panc02 cell membrane camouflage. The formed nanorobots exhibit precise tumor accumulation via homologous targeting and deep penetration through NIR-induced thermophoresis and gas generation propulsion. Within the TME, nanorobots initiate cascade catalysis that generates toxic hydroxyl radicals and depletes glutathione to exaggerate oxidative stress while replenishing oxygen to alleviate tumor hypoxia and amplify photodynamic therapy (PDT). Meanwhile, NIR-triggered photothermal therapy (PTT) accelerates the nanozymatic activity for enhanced catalytic therapy, and PDT-triggered NO forms peroxynitrite (ONOO-) to degrade the extracellular matrix. This establishes a self-amplifying feedback loop for enhanced intratumoral infiltration and overall therapeutic efficacy. Comprehensive evaluations in subcutaneous and orthotopic PC models confirmed that rCeGLI@PM achieved superior therapeutic outcomes through synergistic PTT/PDT/gas/catalytic therapy. In summary, the strategic asymmetrical decoration of multifunctional dendrimers on nanozymes establishes a facile and versatile paradigm for engineering self-propelled nanorobots capable of multimodal synergistic therapies.

title: Lactarius hatsudake Tanaka Polysaccharides Inhibit Hepatocellular Carcinoma by Modulating the Gut Microbiota and Its Metabolites.
abstract: We previously reported that Lactarius hatsudake Tanaka polysaccharide (LHP) can inhibit hepatocellular carcinoma, but the mechanism remains unclear especially gut microbe-mediated antitumor immunity. This research found that LHP and fecal microbiota transplantation were associated with reduced tumor growth. The ratio of CD8+/CD4+ T cells and levels of interferon-γ were increased following LHP intervention in the tumor, spleen, and blood. Additionally, in vivo and in vitro microbiome analyses indicated that LHP treatment significantly increased beneficial bacteria such as Bifidobacterium animalis while reducing Lactobacillus murinus. Furthermore, metabolomic analyses suggested that LHP may be metabolized into propionate via the succinate pathway, accompanied by changes in the microbial composition, which significantly inhibit the arginine and tryptophan metabolic pathways. These microbial and metabolite changes paralleled improvements in the tumor immune microenvironment and coincided with attenuated hepatocellular carcinoma progression. These findings suggest that LHP-induced gut microbiota remodeling is associated with antitumor immune modulation.
journal: Journal of agricultural and food chemistry

title: A Near-Infrared-II Antibody-Photosensitizer Conjugate for Photoimmunotherapy of Advanced Pancreatic Cancer.
abstract: Pancreatic cancer (PC) is a highly lethal malignancy, characterized by frequent late-stage diagnosis and limited response to available treatments. Photoimmunotherapy, which combines the localized tumor ablation of phototherapy with the systemic immune activation of immunotherapy, presents a promising strategy. However, its success is often hampered by insufficient accumulation of therapeutic agents at the tumor site. To address this challenge, we developed a novel antibody-photosensitizer conjugate, named αPD-L1@AIE, by conjugating a multifunctional phototheranostic agent with αPD-L1 antibody for targeted photoimmunotherapy of PC. The incorporation of αPD-L1 not only facilitates tumor-specific targeting but also acts as an immune checkpoint inhibitor. Upon 660 nm laser irradiation, this phototheranostic agent enables NIR-II fluorescence imaging and simultaneously induces potent immunogenic cell death (ICD) via combined photodynamic and photothermal therapy. Following localized phototherapy, the released tumor-associated antigens from ICD initiate a robust antitumor immune response. Such a response is synergistically amplified by αPD-L1, which together alleviates immunosuppression via Treg cell depletion and M2-like macrophage repolarization, thereby promoting a marked increase in cytotoxic T lymphocyte infiltration and granzyme B production. Consequently, the aforementioned photoimmunotherapy approach effectively suppresses tumor growth and inhibits spontaneous metastasis, demonstrating a powerful and transformative paradigm for advanced PC management.

title: TRIP13 Promotes Aflatoxin B1-Induced Hepatocellular Carcinoma Progression by Inhibiting Ferroptosis.
abstract: Aflatoxin B1 (AFB1) is a potent foodborne hepatocarcinogen that contributes substantially to the global burden of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), yet the molecular mechanisms underlying AFB1-driven HCC progression remain incompletely understood. In this study, we identified thyroid hormone receptor-interacting protein 13 (TRIP13) as an important contributor to AFB1-related HCC progression and investigated its involvement in ferroptosis regulation. TCGA-LIHC, GSE25844, and single-cell RNA sequencing data (GSE166635) revealed that TRIP13 was significantly upregulated in AFB1-related HCC, enriched in malignant cell populations, and associated with poor clinical outcomes. In Huh7 cells, AFB1 treatment markedly increased TRIP13 expression, while TRIP13 knockdown significantly suppressed AFB1-induced cell proliferation, colony formation, migration, and epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT). Bulk RNA sequencing and pathway enrichment analyses indicated that TRIP13 overexpression was strongly associated with ferroptosis-related signaling. Mechanistically, TRIP13 was associated with ferroptosis resistance through modulation of the KEAP1/NRF2/xCT/GPX4 pathway, thereby contributing to redox homeostasis during AFB1 exposure. Consistently, TRIP13 knockdown restored ferroptotic sensitivity, as evidenced by increased Fe2+ and malondialdehyde levels and altered glutathione metabolism. Importantly, ferroptosis induction with RSL3 effectively reversed the pro-tumor effects of TRIP13 overexpression both in vitro and in vivo, including enhanced proliferation, EMT, migration, and xenograft tumor growth. Collectively, these findings suggest that TRIP13 contributes to AFB1-associated HCC progression through ferroptosis-related regulation and highlight the AFB1/TRIP13/ferroptosis axis as a potential molecular mechanism and candidate target for further investigation in AFB1-related HCC.

title: Glypican-3-targeted pH-responsive dual-drug co-loaded nanoliposomes for precision combined chemotherapy and anti-metastasis of hepatocellular carcinoma.
abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) chemotherapy is limited by poor drug selectivity, severe systemic toxicity, and frequent drug resistance. This study aimed to construct a novel pH-responsive nanoliposome system co-loaded with paclitaxel (PTX) and doxorubicin (ADR), functionalized with anti-glypican-3 (GPC3) antibodies, for precision combined chemotherapy and anti-metastasis of HCC.Methods: PTX-loaded nanoliposomes were first prepared via reverse evaporation, followed by co-loading with ADR and bovine serum albumin to form PTX-ADR-BNP. GPC3 antibodies were conjugated onto the surface to obtain GPC3-PTX-ADR-BNP. The system was evaluated for particle size, zeta potential, encapsulation efficiency, and pH-responsive release. Cytotoxicity was assessed against HCC and normal cells. In vivo antitumor efficacy, biosafety, and anti-metastatic effects were evaluated using subcutaneous xenograft and lung metastasis models.Results: GPC3-PTX-ADR-BNP exhibited uniform particle size (~180 nm), high encapsulation efficiencies (>96% for PTX, >95% for ADR), and pH-responsive release (~80% at pH 5.3 within 16 h, slow release at pH 7.4). In vitro, it showed potent cytotoxicity against MHCC97H and HuH-7 cells (half-maximal inhibitory concentration: 41.21 and 54.19 μg/mL) with minimal toxicity to normal cells. In vivo, the system prolonged plasma half-life, enhanced tumor accumulation, and achieved >59% tumor inhibition. Biosafety assessments, including hemolysis (<1% at all tested concentrations), serum biochemistry, hematological parameters, and histopathological examination of major organs, showed no significant toxicity compared to the control group. In the pulmonary metastasis model, it effectively suppressed lung metastasis, outperforming free drug and non-targeted groups.Conclusion: GPC3-PTX-ADR-BNP integrates GPC3-mediated active targeting with pH-responsive release for efficient anti-tumor and anti-metastatic effects, with high biocompatibility and low toxicity, offering a promising strategy for precision HCC therapy.

title: Prognostic value of microRNA expression in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) ranks among the deadliest malignancies, with limited survival benefits despite recent therapeutic advances. Few prognostic biomarkers are available for PDAC monitoring in clinical practice. We conducted a meta-analysis to evaluate and synthesise evidence on the prognostic significance of miRNA expression in PDAC.
METHODS: The protocol was registered with PROSPERO (CRD42023463542). We conducted a systematic search in PubMed, CENTRAL, and Embase on January 27, 2026, to identify studies assessing miRNA expression levels in patients with PDAC with reported overall survival (OS) or progression-free survival (PFS) outcomes. Hazard ratios (HRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were pooled using a random-effects model. Prediction intervals (PI) were reported if feasible. Separate analyses were performed by miRNA functional categories: oncogenic, tumour suppressor, chemoresistance-related, metastasis-related, and dual-role miRNAs.
FINDINGS: A total of 142 studies, including 13,824 patients, were included. High expression of oncogenic miRNAs was associated with worse univariate OS (HR 1.70, 95% CI 1.38-2.10; 95% PI 0.63-4.57) and PFS (HR 2.25, 95% CI 1.63-3.10; 95% PI 1.11-4.55). High expression of chemoresistance-related miRNAs was associated with worse multivariate OS (HR 2.11, 95% CI 1.68-2.66; 95% PI 0.96-4.68) and PFS (HR 2.51, 95% CI 1.89-3.33; 95% PI 1.58-3.97). Between-study heterogeneity varied substantially across pooled analyses (I2 range 0-94%). miRNA-21 was the most frequently studied individual biomarker and showed a consistent association with worse multivariate OS (HR 2.24, 95% CI 1.95-2.57; 95% PI 1.92-2.61).
INTERPRETATION: Elevated expression of oncogenic and chemoresistance-related miRNAs is associated with worse survival outcomes in PDAC. However, substantial heterogeneity and wide prediction intervals observed in several pooled analyses indicate variability in effect sizes across studies. Among the investigated biomarkers, miRNA-21 has shown the most consistent prognostic association and may represent the strongest candidate for future clinical implementation. Further validation and standardisation are required before miRNA profiling can be integrated into routine clinical practice.
FUNDING: None to declare.

title: Microbiology-guided antimicrobial prophylaxis, surgical site infection and delivery of adjuvant chemotherapy after resection of perihilar cholangiocarcinoma.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Surgical site infection (SSI) is the dominant morbidity after resection of perihilar cholangiocarcinoma (pCCA). Preoperative biliary instrumentation results in biliary colonisation with antimicrobial-resistant microorganisms, limiting the effectiveness of standard perioperative prophylaxis. Whether microbiology-guided prophylaxis improves outcomes, and whether sepsis compromises adjuvant chemotherapy delivery, is unknown.
METHODS: Retrospective cohort study of consecutive patients undergoing resection of pCCA at a UK tertiary centre (2009-2026). Routine intraoperative bile culture informed changes in institutional antimicrobial prophylaxis in 2019 from cefuroxime and metronidazole to teicoplanin and piperacillin-tazobactam. The primary outcome was SSI. In patients resected from April 2017, when adjuvant capecitabine became routine, chemotherapy receipt and timing were compared by SSI status.
RESULTS: Seventy-four patients were managed prior to the revised protocol and 58 thereafter. Biliary colonisation was near-universal (92 vs. 88%). Resistance to cefuroxime/metronidazole was detected in 70% of culture-positive baseline patients, and 14% for the revised regimen. SSI fell from 42/74 (57%) to 17/58 (29%; p = 0.003), driven by organ/space infections (46 vs. 24%; p = 0.033), and remained associated with the revised protocol after adjustment (OR 0.31, 95% CI 0.13-0.72). Among 67 post-BILCAP-era patients, chemotherapy began within 12 weeks in 16% with SSI compared to 50% without; among recipients, median time to first cycle was 104 vs. 78 days (p = 0.010).
CONCLUSIONS: Microbiology-guided prophylaxis was associated with clinically meaningful reductions in SSI. Reducing septic complications does not just limit perioperative morbidity, but avoids delay in adjuvant chemotherapy.
journal: European journal of surgical oncology : the journal of the European Society of Surgical Oncology and the British Association of Surgical Oncology

title: Targeted inhibition of HK2 expression in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma reprogrammes the immune microenvironment by regulating CCL5-mediated CD8+ T cell infiltration.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is highly resistant to immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) therapy due to its highly immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME).
METHODS: Key regulatory genes were screened using bioinformatics analysis of TCGA and KEGG datasets. The expression patterns of HK2 were analyzed by single-cell sequencing and immunohistochemistry. The HK2-CCL5-CD8+ T-cell axis was evaluated using mouse pancreatic cancer models, in vitro co-culture systems, Transwell assays, RNA sequencing, and flow cytometry. The relationship between HK2 and anti-PD-1 therapy was also assessed.
RESULTS: Hexokinase 2 (HK2), a rate-limiting enzyme of glycolysis, is a key regulator in tumor immune evasion. HK2 is highly expressed in PDAC tumor cells. Its expression is significantly associated with CD8+ T-cell infiltration in the tumor microenvironment and disease progression. Inhibiting HK2 expression significantly promotes CC motif chemokine ligand 5 (CCL5) secretion by pancreatic cancer cells, which enhances the recruitment of CD8+ T-cell. Moreover, inhibiting HK2 enhance antitumor efficacy of anti-PD-1 therapy in PDAC. Mechanistically, ROS scavenging with NAC reverses the CCL5 upregulation caused by HK2 inhibition, which in turn affects CD8+ T-cell infiltration.
CONCLUSION: Our study reveals a novel HK2-CCL5 axis that regulates CD8+ T-cell recruitment and shapes the immune microenvironment in PDAC.

title: tsRNAs in HCC: Biology, liquid biopsy and therapy.
abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is a leading cause of cancer-related death worldwide, and there is an urgent need for non-invasive diagnostic tools and effective treatments. Transfer RNA-derived small RNAs (tsRNAs) are a novel class of small non-coding RNAs generated by site-specific cleavage of transfer RNAs. This review summarizes the biogenesis, classification and biological functions of tsRNAs, focusing on their roles in HCC. tsRNAs contribute to multiple cancer hallmarks, including proliferation, resistance to apoptosis, immune modulation, angiogenesis, metastasis, and metabolic reprogramming, through the regulation of signaling pathways, epigenetic control, and translational regulation. Because tsRNAs are highly stable in body fluids, they represent promising liquid biopsy markers. Several specific tsRNAs have shown excellent diagnostic performance, with area under the curve (AUC) values above 0.84 and improved sensitivity when combined with conventional markers such as alpha-fetoprotein (AFP). Preclinical evidence using antagomirs or agomirs to target oncogenic or tumor-suppressive tsRNAs has demonstrated encouraging anti-tumor effects in HCC models. tsRNAs are emerging as valuable diagnostic biomarkers and potential therapeutic targets for HCC. Clinical translation still faces challenges including low delivery efficiency, off-target effects, and a lack of standardized protocols. Future efforts should focus on unified nomenclature, standardized detection methods, and combination strategies with immunotherapy and targeted therapy to advance precision hepatology.
